title: Spring's longing
hook: in the spring months the bride hears the koel and longs for the Beloved (Tukhari Barah Maha)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nanak's twelve months, and your line was nanak's months. Did you find this month's name, and what it's teaching you to wait for? Today the year begins in earnest. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-four.

A bird calls from a mango tree, early, before the house is awake. Then again, from a little farther off. The poem names it: the koel, singing in the mango tree. Guru Nanak puts it right at the start of his year. The month is Chet, spring, and everything is beautiful. That's the trouble. When the whole world is in bloom, the one thing missing is easier to hear. Today: spring's longing, and a bird that won't stop calling.
screen: `A BIRD IN THE MANGO TREE.` → `CHET: EVERYTHING IN BLOOM.` → `THE MISSING ONE IS LOUDER.`

segments.voice: Here's Chet, given in plain English, not word for word. Chet is good, spring is lovely, the bumblebees are beautiful. The forest is in flower. Then the koel. It sings sweetly in the mango tree, and the bride asks: how can I bear this pain inside me? The bumblebee circles the flowering branch, and she says, how can I live, mother? I'm dying. Notice what's happening. The poem doesn't call spring bad. It calls it good, even lovely. The bird isn't wrong to sing. But beauty, when the one you love is far away, can hurt more than gray skies would. Every lovely thing becomes a reminder of who isn't there to see it. Then the year moves to Vaisakh, and the trees join in. Again in plain English: Vaisakh is good, and the branches put on new clothes. Fresh leaves, like a new outfit for a wedding. And the bride stands looking at the door. Come home, Beloved, she says, have mercy. Carry me across this hard ocean. Without You, I'm not worth half a shell. In Sikh reading, the bride is the soul, and the Beloved is God. So spring here isn't only about weather. It's about the moment life is fullest around you, and something in you still says: not yet. Not without You. The bird keeps calling, and the poem lets it. It doesn't shush the longing. It treats the ache as part of love, the sign that the bride hasn't forgotten who she's waiting for. That's today's line: the bird calls.
screen: `CHET: THE KOEL IN THE MANGO TREE.` · `BEAUTY CAN MAKE MISSING LOUDER.` · `VAISAKH: BRANCHES IN NEW CLOTHES.` · `THE BRIDE WATCHES THE DOOR.` · then, large: `THE BIRD CALLS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen for a bird. If you can, open a window or step outside. If not, just listen to the room. Sit, and let your breath slow. Wait for a bird, any bird, near or far. If one calls, follow the sound until it fades. If none comes, notice the waiting itself: the leaning-in, the small hope. That leaning is the bride at the door. Let it be there without hurrying it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru softly between the calls. The bell holds the time.
Spring's longing. In Guru Nanak's Chet and Vaisakh, the koel sings and the trees put on new clothes, and all that beauty makes the absent Beloved felt more. Today's word.
Your line: the bird calls. Today, whenever you hear a bird, let it remind you of one person or one hope you're waiting on. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-four.

howItsDone: Sikhs sing Guru Nanak's Barah Maha in kirtan and read it as part of the Guru Granth Sahib, hearing the bride's longing in each month as the soul's longing for God.

original.note: kokil: the koel, the bird that sings in the mango tree in Nanak's Chet.

trapdoor: what you thought: a spring poem about flowers and birds.
what it means: the fullest season makes the missing Beloved felt most; the bride is the soul longing for God.
what a scholar hears: some readers hear an echo of folk love songs in the koel in the mango tree, turned here into the soul's cry.
recall: the letter S, the Patti's first
